page.overview:
Who is M. Bison?

Black (pre-Street Fighter V)White (Street Fighter V onward)

M. Bison, known as in Japan, is a video game character and the main antagonist of the Street Fighter series, first appearing as the non-playable final boss in Street Fighter II before becoming playable in its update, Street Fighter II: Champion Edition. The founder and leader of the powerful criminal organization Shadaloo, he is a self-imposed dictator and megalomaniac seeking world domination. In his character arcade mode in Street Fighter 6, he was addressed as the Nameless Man.

M. Bison was created for Street Fighter II in 1989 after Akira Nishitani asked for an evil overlord with powers beyond mortal comprehension. M. Bison and his design were inspired by two manga villains who are insane but formidable Japanese imperialist dictators with katana swords: [https://rikioh.fandom.com/wiki/Washizaki Washizaki], a supporting antagonist from Riki-Oh; and [https://villains.fandom.com/wiki/Yasunori_Kato Yasunori Katō], the antagonist from Tokyo: The Last Megalopolis (aka ., with M. Bison's Street Fighter II portrait being traced over an image of Washizaki from a page in the Riki-Oh: Cape Arc manga (Vol. 4, Ch. 22, Pg. 26), the name "Washizaki" itself was also used as a development placeholder for the Shadaloo Dictator before trademarking the character's official name(s).

M. Bison's steel-made shinguards are based off of the style used in the Universal Wrestling Federation of Japan during the mid-1980s. His uniform highly resembles the Japanese and Chinese Imperial uniforms in red, as per his inspirational sources, with some possible influences from the uniforms worn by SS officers of Nazi Germany; the winged skull on his visor cap and the first letter of Shadaloo on his belt is shaped as a single Sig rune. The prominent use of all uniform red and the Nazism influences may hearken to the term derogatory phrase "communazi" or "commie nazi", which was coined by an American reporter in 1939 and popularized by Time Magazine to describe the bare differences communism and nazism had around the beginning of World War II, and was used in the wake of the Cold War by the United States of America to justify the USSR as being "a dictatorship in equivalence in all but name". After the Cold War, "commie nazi" would become lampooning of US action movies and their decline into the 1990s utilizing foreign villains as but punching bags for deep seated and nationalism veering entertainment, as popularized by The Simpsons and depicted in the Season 9 episode "King of the Hill" from the in-show movie series, McBain, and to a relatable extent, lampoons Guile and Charlie in this regard.
